text: Time to put Chapter 1 together. You've been brought in to implement Incident Management for a 500-person manufacturing company standing up its first ServiceNow instance, and the service desk lead hands you four real requirements.

Enforce the state model so nothing closes without evidence, calculate Priority instead of hand-picking it, route Network incidents automatically and spread them across the team, and set a real threshold for when an incident becomes a Major Incident.

First, the state model. The complaint was agents closing tickets with nothing written down about what fixed them. A Data Policy conditioned on Resolved makes Resolution Code and Close Notes mandatory, and blocks the jump from New straight to Closed. You verify it by actually trying both bad transitions and confirming the platform refuses them — not by just reading the configuration and assuming it works.

Second, Priority. Before touching the lookup rule matrix, you confirm with the business what Impact 1, 2, and 3 actually mean to them — Impact 1 is affects the whole plant floor, not just feels urgent. Then you populate the grid so Priority 1 only results from Impact 1 and Urgency 1 together, and every manual override gets logged instead of silently drifting from the calculated value.

Third, routing. A flow triggered on Incident Created checks for Category equals Network and sets Assignment Group to Network Operations. Because that group has six agents, you configure round robin distribution so new incidents rotate across the team instead of piling onto whoever's name sorts first.

Fourth, the Major Incident threshold. You don't tie it to Priority alone, because a single Priority 1 affecting one person's laptop shouldn't trigger a war room. The threshold is Priority 1 and affecting more than 50 users, which flags the incident as a Candidate — a human still makes the actual Declared call.

State enforcement verified, Priority calculated, Network incidents routed and distributed, and a real Major Incident threshold in place. Chapter 2 picks up from here: the Problem table, and its relationship to the incidents you've just learned to implement.
